title: Five colors
hook: the five colors blind the eye; the sage cares for the belly, not the eye (Tao Te Ching 12)

segments.voice: Yesterday, thirty spokes, and the hole in the hub that lets the wheel turn. Your line was the empty center. Did you leave a gap open, and did anything move through it? Day one thousand seventy-four.

A phone screen at the end of a long day. Red badges. A video that starts on its own. A banner sliding down over the banner you were reading. Three tabs of music, two of them playing. None of it is evil. Some of it is even interesting. And yet, after an hour of it, a slice of plain toast can taste like nothing, and a quiet room can feel strangely loud. An old Chinese book, written long before any screen, has a short chapter about exactly this kind of tired. Chapter twelve of the Tao Te Ching.
screen: `RED BADGES, AUTOPLAY, BANNERS.` → `TOAST TASTES LIKE NOTHING.` → `CHAPTER TWELVE.`

segments.voice: First, the list. The chapter says the five colors blind the eye. The five notes deafen the ear. The five flavors dull the mouth. Racing and hunting drive the mind wild. Goods that are hard to get lead people astray. It's a list of good things: color, music, food, excitement, treasure. The problem isn't any one of them. The problem is what too much of them does to the senses that take them in. Second, notice the strange result. More color, and you see less. More sound, and you hear less. The senses don't get sharper with more input; in the chapter's picture, they go numb. It's the plain toast after the sugar, the quiet room after the loud one. Third, the turn. So, the chapter says, the sage cares for the belly and not the eye. The belly here isn't about overeating. Some translators read it as what a person actually needs, set against what only dazzles. The eye wants more to look at. The belly wants enough. Then the chapter ends with a short instruction: let go of that, take hold of this. It doesn't spell out which is which. Some readers fill it in: that is the dazzle, this is the plain need underneath. Fourth, what it isn't saying. It isn't telling anyone to hate color or give up music. Read this way, the chapter is about the volume knob, not the radio: turn it down, and the senses can come back.
screen: `FIVE COLORS BLIND THE EYE.` · `MORE TO SEE, AND YOU SEE LESS.` · `THE BELLY, NOT THE EYE.` · `THE VOLUME KNOB, NOT THE RADIO.` · then, large: `LET GO OF THAT. TAKE HOLD OF THIS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: turn down one stimulation. Right now, pick one thing. Put the phone face down, or in another room. Turn off the music, or the second screen, or dim a bright light. Then sit for two minutes with less coming in. Notice what the senses do once they're not being flooded. Maybe a sound you hadn't heard. A color in the room that was there all along. The taste in your mouth. Nothing to chase, just less to see. The bell holds the time.
Five colors. Chapter twelve's picture of too much: color, sound and flavor that, piled up, leave the senses numb. Today's word.
Your line: less to see. Choose one hour today with one input turned off, the radio in the car, the second screen, the badges, and notice what comes back. Day one thousand seventy-four.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter twelve as a reason to simplify their surroundings for a while: fewer screens, less noise, plainer food, to let the senses recover.

trapdoor: what you thought: five colors is about painting.
what it means: color, sound, flavor and excitement, piled up, leave the senses numb; the sage chooses what's needed over what dazzles.
what a scholar hears: belly and eye stand for need and appetite; the closing line, let go of that, take hold of this, is left for the reader to fill in.

notes: Chapter 12 paraphrased throughout (Legge's 1891 version of this chapter is in rhymed verse, and the exact wording was not quoted). Confirm the list: five colors blind, five notes deafen, five flavors dull the palate, racing and hunting madden the mind, rare goods hinder conduct; the sage is for the belly, not the eye; 'he puts away that and takes this' (去彼取此).
Belly/eye glossed as need versus what dazzles, attributed to 'some translators'. Confirm.
Day 1065 (Empty minds, full bellies) covered chapter 3's 'fills their bellies'; this day frames the belly as need versus dazzle, not as feeding the people.
Editor pass: the closing 'turn it down, and the senses come back' is now framed as a reading rather than stated as the chapter's claim.
